title: Water: where rain goes, and where our tap water comes from
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 3 'Water — A Precious Gift' (rain, storing and cleaning water, using it at home, problems of water quality and quantity, saving water). No textbook needed.
summary: When rain lands, it soaks into the ground, runs off, or evaporates into the air. Your child measures rain with a home-made gauge, sees water soak in or run off, and builds a well in a jar to see groundwater. They trace their tap water back to its source and count how many litres the family uses in a day. They test why a clay pot keeps water cool, and clean muddy water to find that clear water can still carry germs. They end by setting out water for birds and making a family plan to save water.
builds_on: This is the first water rung. Your child already knows, from Class 1 and 2 science, that plants and animals need water. In Class 5 the water rung goes much further: the full water cycle with condensation and transpiration, how little of Earth's water is fresh, how rivers carve the land, freshwater habitats and food chains, and how villages and cities can catch and share rain.
goals: By the end your child can measure rain with a home-made rain gauge and keep a sky diary.
By the end your child can say the three things rain does when it lands (soaks in, runs off, dries up) and show which surfaces let it soak in.
By the end your child can explain groundwater and how a well or borewell gets its water.
By the end your child can trace the water in their home back to its source and estimate how many litres the family uses in a day.
By the end your child can show three ways of cleaning water and explain why water that looks clear may still carry germs.
By the end your child can suggest ways to reuse and save water, and say why water is shared by every living thing, not only people.

words: rain gauge
a container with a scale that measures how much rain has fallen
absorb
to soak up, the way soil or a sponge soaks up water
run-off
rainwater that flows away over the ground instead of soaking in
evaporate
when liquid water slowly turns into water vapour, an invisible gas in the air
groundwater
water stored under the ground in the gaps between grains of soil, sand and rock
borewell
a deep, narrow hole drilled to pump up groundwater
source
the place where something comes from
filter
something that lets water through but catches dirt
germs
living things too small to see, some of which make us ill
grey water
water already used for washing that can be used again for some jobs
conserve
to use carefully so there is enough for later and for others
commons
something that belongs to everyone together, like air, a village pond or a river

days.title: Where does our water come from?
days.goal: Hook your child with the rain, meet the story, and start measuring and watching water.

steps.title: My water morning
steps.do: Ask your child to list every time they used water since waking up: brushing, the toilet, washing hands, drinking, the water in their coffee or milk, the water that cooked the rice or steamed the idli. Count them on your fingers. Say: 'Every drop of that water came from somewhere. This week we find out where.'

steps.title: Story: The Frog Who Looked Up
steps.do: Read the story aloud slowly. It is about a frog living in a dry well in Rajasthan. Don't explain it. Ask two of the story questions: 'Where did the frog think water came from?' and 'Where did the water really come from in the end?' Write down what your child says. You will come back to it on Day 2.

steps.title: Make a rain gauge and sky diary
steps.do: Do Activity a1. A grown-up cuts the top off a clear plastic bottle. Put a few pebbles in the bottom and add water up to a line. Mark that line 0, so the curved base doesn't spoil the reading. Stick a paper ruler on the side, starting at 0. Turn the cut top upside down into the bottle, as a funnel. Put it on an open terrace or balcony ledge, away from walls, roofs and trees. Start the sky diary: draw today's sky, and write the date and the gauge reading. Say: 'Weather scientists all over India read rain gauges like this every morning.'

steps.title: Sun or shade: set up the vanishing water
steps.do: Set up Experiment e1. Pour exactly two spoons of water on each of two steel plates, and wet two hankies the same amount. Put one plate and one hanky in the sun, and the others in the shade. Ask your child which will dry first, and where the water will go. Write the guesses in the sky diary.

need: a ruler or paper scale and tape
a notebook for the sky diary

days.title: Where does the rain go?
days.goal: See rain soak in, run off and dry up, and find the hidden water under the ground.

steps.title: Sun and shade results
steps.do: Look at Experiment e1. Ask: 'Which plate dried first? Where did the water go? Did it go through the plate?' (No. It turned into water vapour, an invisible gas, and went into the air. This is called evaporation. The sun's heat makes it faster.) Read the rain gauge and fill in the sky diary.

steps.title: Rain on four surfaces
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Pour half a mug of water slowly on each surface: the soil in a big potted plant, a tray of sand, and the bathroom floor tiles. If there is a park nearby, also try bare soil, grass and a cement path. For each one, ask: 'Did the water soak in, run off, or make a puddle?' Your child fills in the table in the sky diary. Ask: 'In a city with roads and roofs everywhere, where does the rain go?' (Most of it runs off into drains. Very little soaks in.)

steps.title: A well in a jar
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Stand a straw against the inside of a clear jar, touching the bottom. Fill the jar with small stones, then sand, then soil. Pour a cup of water on top, like rain. Watch it sink into the soil and collect in the gaps at the bottom. Say: 'This is groundwater. It is not an underground lake. It sits in the tiny gaps between grains, like water in a sponge.' Then your child sucks gently on the straw, like a well pump, and watches the water level at the bottom drop.

steps.title: Make a rainstorm with your hands
steps.do: Sit in a circle (two people is enough). The leader starts and everyone copies: rub palms together (a breeze), click fingers (first drops), pat thighs (heavy rain), stamp feet and pat thighs (a downpour). Then go back down the same steps to silence. Ask: 'Where did all that rain go after the storm?' (Some soaked in, some ran off, and some will evaporate.)

steps.title: Back to the frog
steps.do: Ask again: 'Where did the water in the frog's well really come from?' (From rain that soaked into the ground nearby and seeped into the well from the sides and the bottom.) Ask: 'Why did the well fill only after the women of the village rebuilt the johad, the bank of earth?' (It slowed the rain down, so it had time to soak in instead of running away.)

need: the rain gauge and sky diary
a mug of water, a potted plant and a tray of sand
a clear jar or cut bottle

days.title: Follow the pipe
days.goal: Trace your home's water back to where it really comes from, and notice who brings it.

steps.title: Sky diary
steps.do: Read the rain gauge and fill in the sky diary. If it hasn't rained, look at the weather report in the newspaper or on a phone. It says how many millimetres of rain fell in your city.

steps.title: The great pipe trail
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Start at the kitchen tap and follow the pipe as far as you can see it: through the wall, to the overhead tank, down to the sump, the borewell or the city pipe. Your child draws the trail as a map with arrows. Ask: 'And where does the water get into that pipe?' Help them finish the map: a river, lake or dam far away, groundwater pumped up by a borewell, or a tanker. Chennai, for example, gets much of its water from lakes like Chembarambakkam and Puzhal. If you don't know, phone your building's caretaker or plumber together and ask.

steps.title: Who brings the water?
steps.do: Ask: 'In our home, who makes sure there is water? Who fills the bottles, switches on the motor, calls the tanker?' Then say: 'In many villages in India, people still walk to a well, a pond or a handpump every day and carry water home. Most of this carrying is done by women and girls, sometimes for hours.' Ask: 'How would your day change if you had to fetch all the water you used this morning?' Listen. Don't push an answer.

steps.title: Reading the land for hidden water
steps.do: Tell voice v4, about Varahamihira, who wrote how plants, termite mounds and the colour of soil can show where water is underground. Ask the voice question. Then say: 'Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in Meghalaya get more than ten metres of rain in a year. Chennai gets about one and a half metres, most of it from October to December. Parts of the Thar desert in Rajasthan get less than the height of your hand.' Ask: 'If you lived in the desert, how would you make sure you had water all year?' (Catch every drop when it rains, store it, and use it carefully.) You'll see how people did this on Day 5.

need: a phone to ask the caretaker or panchayat (optional)

days.title: How much water do we really use?
days.goal: Count the family's water in litres and find out how a small drip adds up.

steps.title: Guess the litres
steps.do: Show a 1-litre bottle. Ask: 'How many of these bottles do you think our whole family uses in one day?' Write the guess in big numbers and keep it. Most children guess 10 or 20.

steps.title: Start the water audit
steps.do: Do Activity a3. First, measure how many litres your mug and bucket hold, by filling them from the 1-litre bottle. A flush tank often has its size marked, usually 6 to 10 litres. Then make the audit chart. Write one row for each job: brushing, bathing, toilet, cooking, drinking, washing dishes, washing clothes, mopping the floor. For the next 24 hours, each time someone uses water, they add a tally mark in that row. Your child is the auditor.

steps.title: Drop detective
steps.do: Do the drip test in Activity a3. Open a tap so it just drips. Put a cup under it for exactly 10 minutes. Measure the water with a spoon or a measuring cup. There are six lots of 10 minutes in an hour, so multiply by 6. Then multiply by 24 for a whole day. Ask: 'How much would one dripping tap waste in a day? In a year?' (Often several litres a day.)

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1 together: rain, soaking in, groundwater and sources. Read each question aloud if needed. For the written questions, accept any answer with a real reason.

days.title: Storing water: then and now
days.goal: Total the audit, test the clay pot, and meet the people who built India's water stores.

steps.title: Audit total
steps.do: Add up the family's audit together. For each row, multiply the tally marks by the litres, then add all the rows. Compare the total with the guess from Day 4. Say: 'Water planners in Indian cities allow 135 litres per person each day. Many families in dry villages manage on 40 litres or less.' Ask: 'Which job used the most water? Which one could we easily use less for?'

steps.title: Why is water in a clay pot cool?
steps.do: Do Experiment e4. In the morning, fill a clay pot (a matka, or a mann panai as it is called in Tamil Nadu) and a steel bottle from the same tap. Keep them side by side in a shady, airy place. After a few hours, your child dips a finger in each, or uses a thermometer if you have one. Then wrap a wet cloth around the steel bottle and check again an hour later. If you have no clay pot, use two steel bottles and wrap one in a wet cloth from the start. Ask: 'Why is the clay pot cooler?' (Water seeps through tiny holes in the clay and evaporates from the outside. Evaporating water takes heat away with it. That is why you feel cold when you come out of a bath.)

steps.title: Stepwells, tanks and temple tanks
steps.do: Tell voice v3. If you have a lavender ₹100 note, show Rani ki Vav on the back. Say: 'A stepwell is a deep well with stairs going down, so people could reach the water even when the level fell in summer.' Then tell your child about two more ways of storing rain. In the Thar desert, families build a tanka, a covered underground tank, with a clean courtyard sloping into it. In Tamil Nadu, villages store rain in big tanks called eris, and many temples have huge stepped tanks, like the Teppakulam in Madurai. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Then and now
steps.do: Ask: 'How did people store water in the past? How do we store it now?' Make a two-column list. Then: clay pot, tanka, stepwell, eri, temple tank, village pond. Now: overhead tank, sump, steel drum, plastic bottle. Ask: 'Which ones need electricity? Which ones keep working if the power goes off?'

steps.title: Sheetali: a cooling breath
steps.do: Show your child sheetali, a cooling breath from yoga. Curl the tongue into a tube, or, if they can't, hold the teeth lightly together. Breathe in slowly through the mouth, then close it and breathe out through the nose. Do it five times. Ask: 'Does your tongue feel cool? Why?' (Air moving over the wet tongue makes water evaporate, which takes heat away, just like the clay pot.)

need: a clay pot, or a second steel bottle

prep.task: Fill the clay pot and the steel bottle from the same tap and keep them side by side

days.title: Clear is not clean
days.goal: Clean muddy water three ways, and find out why clean-looking water can still make people ill.

steps.title: Settle, filter, boil
steps.do: Do Experiment e5. Stir two spoons of soil into a glass of water. Leave it for 10 minutes and watch the mud settle at the bottom. This is called settling. Build a filter from a cut bottle with cloth, sand and small stones. Pour the top water gently through it. Compare the water before and after. Ask: 'Is it safe to drink now?' The answer is no. Say: 'The filter caught the mud, but it can't catch germs. They are far too small to see. To kill germs, we boil the water, or use a proper water purifier.' Never let your child drink the filtered water.

steps.title: The doctor and the pump
steps.do: Tell voice v1, about John Snow and Henry Whitehead. Draw a quick street map with a pump in the middle, and dots for the houses where people fell ill, crowded round the pump. Ask: 'If you were the doctor, what would you think was making people ill?' Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2. It asks your child to use the week's ideas in new places: a desert home, a dripping tap at school, a clay pot.

need: a glass, soil and a spoon
a clean cloth or cotton wool
clean sand and small stones, and activated charcoal from an aquarium shop (optional)

days.title: Using water twice, and sharing it
days.goal: Find water you can reuse, play the water journey game, and think about who water belongs to.

steps.title: Reuse sort at the sink
steps.do: At the kitchen sink, show your child four kinds of used water: water from washing rice or vegetables, water from washing hands with soap, the last rinse of the clothes, and dirty mopping water. For each one, ask: 'Could this be used again? For what?' (Rice and vegetable water can water plants. The last rinse of the clothes can mop the floor or flush the toilet. Soapy or very dirty water goes down the drain.) Choose one reuse your family will really do this week.

steps.title: The ponds are still standing
steps.do: Tell voice v2, about Anupam Mishra. Ask: 'Who do you think built the old ponds and tanks in our town or village? Who looked after them?' (Ordinary people: farmers, masons and the whole village together.) Then ask the voice question.

steps.title: Drop's Journey
steps.do: Play the board game g1. Each player is a raindrop trying to reach the well. Read every square aloud. Your child explains why it sends the drop forward or back, for example: cement makes rain run off, a forest lets it soak in.

steps.title: Start the water-sharing project
steps.do: Begin the project. Choose a shady spot on a balcony, window ledge or terrace for a bird bath. Use a shallow clay dish or the base of a broken pot. Fill it today. Write in the sky diary which visitors come over the next few days.

need: the printed game board, counters and a die
a shallow clay dish or pot base

days.title: Water for whoever comes: check and teach it back
days.goal: Finish the project, try the challenge worksheet, and teach the whole family about water.

steps.title: Bird bath report and our water plan
steps.do: Look at the bird bath list: who came? (Crows, mynas, pigeons, sparrows, squirrels, bees?) Then finish the project. Your child writes a three-point family water plan from the audit, for example: close the tap while brushing, fix the drip, use rice water for plants. Stick it near the sink.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. It has harder 'what if' questions, and asks your child to decide who should get water first. The last section has no single right answer, so listen to the reasons.

steps.title: Check questions
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud. Let your child use the sky diary, the jar well and the audit chart to explain.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches the family for five minutes, using the jar well. They explain where rain goes, where your tap water comes from, why clear water is not always clean, and one way the family will save water. Then ask: 'Who does the rain belong to?'

need: the sky diary and audit chart

worksheets.title: Rain, ground and tap

sections.p: Rain falls on a cement floor. Most of it will…
Rain falls on soft soil with grass. Most of it will…
When water on a hot plate slowly disappears into the air, we say it ____.
Water stored under the ground in the gaps between grains of sand and soil is called ____.

sections: B. Where does our water come from?

sections.p: Match the source to what it is.
pairs: water flowing over the land to the sea
a deep hole drilled to pump up groundwater
a big body of still water on land
a truck that carries water to homes

sections.p: Sort these into places where rain can soak in, and places where it runs off.
Arjun lives in Chennai. After a day of light rain, his rain gauge showed only 2 mm, and the soil in his potted plant was wet. Where did the rest of the rain that fell around him go? Give two places.
Why do you think a city with lots of roads gets more floods in the rain than a village with fields?
You filtered muddy water through sand and cloth. It looks clear. Is it safe to drink?
opts: No, there may be germs too small to see

sections.p: Which of these kills germs in water?
opts: boiling it for a few minutes

sections.p: A clay pot keeps water cool because water seeps out and ____ from its outside, taking heat away.
Which used water could you reuse for plants or mopping, and which should go down the drain?
items: water used to mop a muddy floor
water left in a drinking bottle

sections.p: Match each way of storing water to what it is.
pairs: a covered underground tank in the Thar desert
a deep well with stairs down to the water
a pot that keeps drinking water cool
a big village tank in Tamil Nadu that stores rain
a tank on a roof that sends water down the pipes

sections.p: A tap drips 50 ml in 10 minutes. In one hour it drips ____ ml.
A family in a desert gets rain only on a few days a year. Plan how they could have water all year. Draw or write.
At Farhan's school in Hyderabad, a tap drips all weekend. Who should fix it, and why might nobody do it?
A well in a village dried up after the hills above were made bare and hard. Why?
opts: Bare ground lets rain run away before it can soak in and refill the groundwater
Wells only get water from rain falling straight in

sections.p: Lakshmi and Joseph are neighbours near Bengaluru. Their wells take water from the same groundwater. Joseph digs a much deeper borewell and pumps all day. What might happen?
opts: Nothing, because groundwater never runs out
Lakshmi's shallower well may go dry

sections.p: Rani ki Vav is a stepwell in Gujarat. When the water level fell, people walked down ____ to reach the water.
John Snow was a doctor in London in 1854. He showed that cholera, a deadly illness, was spread by…
Match the person to what they did.
pairs: mapped cholera deaths around a pump
a priest who checked Snow's idea house by house
wrote about the people who built India's ponds

sections.p: A village pond is used by farmers, by buffaloes, by frogs and birds, and by children who swim. In a dry summer there isn't enough for everyone. Who should decide how it is shared, and how? Give reasons.
Some people say water should be free for everyone. Others say people should pay for it so they don't waste it. What do you think? What would happen to a poor family in each case?
How could you test whether a clay pot cools water better in the sun or in the shade? What will you keep the same?

experiments.title: Sun or shade: where does the water go?
experiments.question: Where does water go when it dries up, and does the sun make it go faster?
need: a sunny place and a shady place
steps: Put exactly two spoons of water on each plate.
Wet both hankies and squeeze them the same amount.
Put one plate and one hanky in the sun, the other plate and hanky in the shade.
Check every 30 minutes and note which is dry first.
Next day, talk about where the water went.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which plate will dry first? Will the water go into the plate, the ground or somewhere else?'
experiments.observe: The sunny plate and hanky dry first. No water has gone through the steel.
experiments.why: Liquid water slowly turns into water vapour, an invisible gas that mixes into the air. This is evaporation. Heat from the sun gives the water more energy, so it evaporates faster. The water hasn't been destroyed: it is in the air around us, and one day it will come down as rain again.
experiments.time: 10 min to set up, check over 2–3 hours

experiments.title: Rain on four surfaces
experiments.question: Where does rain go when it lands on different ground?
need: a big potted plant, a tray of sand, and a tiled floor (and bare soil, grass and cement in a park, if you have one nearby)
steps: Pour half a mug slowly on each surface, from the same height.
Watch for 1 minute each.
Record: soaked in, ran off, or made a puddle.
Look again after 30 minutes.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which surface will drink the water fastest? Which will let it run away?'
experiments.observe: The soil and sand soak the water in. The tiles make it run off or puddle, and later it dries up.
experiments.why: Soil and sand have tiny gaps between their grains that water can trickle into. Grass roots make even more channels. Cement and tiles have no gaps, so water runs off into drains or evaporates. That is why paved cities lose most of their rain and flood easily, while forests and fields store it underground.
experiments.safety: Watch out for slippery wet tiles.

experiments.title: A well in a jar
experiments.question: How is water stored under the ground, and how does a well get it?
need: a clear jar or cut-off bottle
small stones, sand and soil (an aquarium shop sells clean gravel and sand)
steps: Stand the straw against the side of the jar, reaching the bottom.
Fill with a layer of small stones, then sand, then soil on top.
Pour a cup of water slowly on top like rain.
Watch it sink and collect between the stones at the bottom.
Suck gently on the straw to pull water up from the bottom, and watch the water level fall.
Pour more 'rain' and watch the level rise again.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Where will the water go? Will we be able to see it?'
experiments.observe: The water disappears from the top and appears as a wet layer at the bottom, filling the gaps between the stones. Sucking it out lowers it, and more rain raises it.
experiments.why: Groundwater is not usually a big underground lake. It fills the tiny spaces between grains of soil, sand and rock, like water in a sponge. A well or borewell is a hole that reaches down into this wet layer. If we pump faster than rain soaks in to refill it, the level falls and wells dry up.
experiments.safety: Use clean sand and stones. Don't drink the water.

experiments.title: Why does a clay pot keep water cool?
experiments.question: Does water stay cooler in a clay pot than in a steel bottle?
need: a clay pot (a matka or a mann panai), or a second steel bottle
steps: In the morning, fill both from the same tap.
Keep them side by side in a shady, airy spot.
After a few hours, feel the water in each (or measure).
Feel the outside of the clay pot: is it damp?
Wrap a wet cloth round the steel bottle and test again after an hour. If you have no clay pot, compare two steel bottles, one wrapped in a wet cloth.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which will be cooler? Why might that be?'
experiments.observe: The water in the clay pot is cooler, and the outside of the pot is damp. The bottle with a wet cloth also gets cooler.
experiments.why: Clay has tiny holes. A little water seeps through and evaporates from the outside. To evaporate, water needs heat, and it takes that heat from the pot and the water inside, so they cool down. The wet cloth does the same. Your skin works like this too: sweat evaporates and cools you.
experiments.time: 15 min + a few hours of waiting

experiments.title: Settle, filter, boil: how clean is clean?
experiments.question: Can we make muddy water clean, and is clear water safe to drink?
need: a cut plastic bottle with its cap pierced
a clean cloth or cotton wool
clean sand and small stones, and activated charcoal from an aquarium shop (optional)
steps: Stir two spoons of soil into a glass of water.
Leave it for 10 minutes and watch the mud settle.
Build the filter in the upside-down bottle: cloth at the neck, then charcoal if you have it, then sand, then small stones on top.
Pour the top water gently through the filter into a clean glass.
Compare the water before and after.
Talk about why we still don't drink it.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the water come out clear? Will it be safe to drink?'
experiments.observe: Settling makes the top water clearer. The filter makes it clearer still.
experiments.why: Settling lets heavy bits of soil sink. A filter catches bits too big to fit between its grains. But germs, like bacteria and viruses, are so tiny that thousands could fit on a full stop, and many slip through a home filter. Boiling kills them. Water can also carry things dissolved in it that you can't see, like too much fluoride or arsenic in some groundwater. Only a test can find these.
experiments.safety: Never drink the filtered water. Wash hands after handling soil and dirty water.

activities.title: Rain gauge and sky diary
steps: A grown-up cuts the top third off the bottle.
Put pebbles in the bottom and add water up to a line. Mark that line 0.
Tape the scale on the side starting at 0.
Turn the top upside down into the bottle as a funnel.
Place it on an open terrace or balcony ledge, away from walls, trees and roofs.
Every morning, read the level, write it in millimetres, draw the sky, then tip the extra water back to 0.
activities.outcome: A working rain gauge and a week of rain readings and sky drawings.

activities.title: The great pipe trail
steps: Start at the kitchen tap.
Follow the pipe through the house as far as you can see.
Find the tank, the sump, the motor, the meter or the handpump.
Draw the trail as a map with arrows.
Find out the source: river, lake, dam, borewell or tanker.
Add where the used water goes: the drain, the sewer, a soak pit or a river.
activities.outcome: A map of the water's journey into and out of your home.

activities.title: Family water audit and drop detective
steps: Measure how many litres a mug, a bucket and a flush hold.
Make a chart of water jobs with tally columns.
For 24 hours, every family member adds a tally each time they use water.
Multiply tallies by litres and add the total.
Drip test: collect drips from a tap for 10 minutes and work out a day's waste.
activities.outcome: The family's real daily water use in litres, and a plan to use less.

voices.who: John Snow (1813–1858), doctor, and Henry Whitehead (1825–1896), curate, London, England
voices.idea: In 1854 cholera killed hundreds of people in the Soho area of London within days. Snow marked the homes of the dead on a street map and saw that most lived near the water pump on Broad Street, and that people who drank from other pumps mostly stayed well. He said cholera was spread by dirty water, not by bad air. Henry Whitehead, a young local priest, thought Snow was wrong and went house to house to prove it, but his careful notes ended up supporting Snow, and he helped find that the outbreak probably began when a sick baby's nappies were washed into a leaking cesspit right next to the well.
voices.then: Most doctors and the city's health board believed diseases came from foul-smelling air (miasma). The pump handle was removed, but an official committee in 1855 did not accept Snow's water idea. In the same year, 1854, the Italian scientist Filippo Pacini saw the cholera germ under a microscope, but almost nobody noticed his work for decades.
voices.now: Accepted. Cholera is caused by a germ (a bacterium) that spreads through water dirtied by human waste. Snow's map is now one of the most famous in science, and Pacini is finally credited in the germ's scientific name, Vibrio cholerae Pacini 1854.
voices.ask: Whitehead set out to prove Snow wrong, but changed his mind. What evidence would make you change your mind about something you are sure of?

voices.who: Anupam Mishra (1948–2016), writer and environmentalist, India
voices.idea: In his book 'Aaj Bhi Khare Hain Talab' (1993), which means 'The Ponds Are Still Standing', Mishra recorded how ordinary communities across India built and looked after ponds, tanks and stepwells for centuries. He wrote down who chose the spot, how the banks were shaped, and how the whole village cleared the silt together each year. He showed that this knowledge belonged to masons, farmers and villagers, not to engineers with degrees.
voices.then: Many town planners in the 20th century saw old ponds as dirty and old-fashioned and expected piped water and borewells to replace them. Many tanks were filled in and built over.
voices.now: Debated. Many towns and villages have revived old tanks and ponds, and they help refill groundwater. But big cities of millions also need dams, pipes and treatment plants. Most experts now say we need both old and new ways working together.
voices.ask: Why might an engineer and a village elder know different things about where water flows? Whose knowledge gets written down?

voices.who: Queen Udayamati and Rani ki Vav, Patan, Gujarat (11th century)
voices.idea: Rani ki Vav, 'the Queen's stepwell', was built under Queen Udayamati in memory of her husband, King Bhima I of the Chaulukya kings. It goes down seven levels of stone stairs to the water, and its walls carry hundreds of carved figures. Stepwells let people reach water even when it fell far below the ground in the dry season.
voices.then: Over the centuries floods filled it with silt and it lay buried and almost forgotten. Archaeologists dug it out and restored it in the 20th century.
voices.now: Accepted. In 2014 it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it is shown on India's ₹100 note. Thousands of stepwells were built across western India, and many of them were paid for by women.
voices.ask: The queen's name is on the stepwell. But who cut the stone, carried it and carved the figures? How could we find out?

voices.idea: In his great book the Brihat Samhita, Varahamihira wrote a whole chapter on finding water under the ground (dakargala). He listed signs to look for: certain trees growing in a dry place, a termite mound near a particular tree, the colour and smell of the soil, plants that stay green when others dry up. Each sign told the well-digger how deep the water might be.
voices.then: For centuries, well-diggers and farmers in India used signs like these, along with their own experience, passed down by word of mouth.
voices.now: Debated. The basic idea is sound. Deep-rooted trees that stay green in a dry place often do point to water nearby, and so can termite mounds, because termites need damp soil. Some Indian geologists have tested a few of his signs and reported that they often worked. Others say the tests were too small to be sure, and that the depths in the book can't be trusted everywhere. Today scientists also use rocks, maps and instruments.
voices.ask: If a green tree grows in a dry field, is it a sign of water, or could there be another reason? How could you test one of Varahamihira's signs fairly?

project.title: Water for whoever comes
steps: Choose a shady spot that cats can't reach easily, and set a shallow clay dish or pot base there.
Fill it every morning with fresh water (only 2–3 cm deep, with a stone in the middle so small birds and bees can stand).
Keep a visitors' list in the sky diary for at least four days.
From the water audit, choose the three biggest ways your family could save water.
Write and decorate a three-point family water plan and stick it near the sink.
After a week, check: did we stick to it? Read the water meter or count buckets again if you can.
project.outcome: A bird bath with a list of visitors, and a family water plan based on real measurements.

game.title: Drop's Journey
need: one counter per player (a seed, button or bead)
rules: Each player is a raindrop. Everyone starts at the cloud (START).
Take turns to roll the die and move.
Read the square aloud and do what it says. Before moving, say why: for example 'cement makes rain run off'.
If you land on a square that sends you back to the cloud, start again from START.
The first drop to reach the WELL wins. Play again and see if anyone can reach it without being sent back.
squares: START: you fall from a cloud
You land on a forest: soak in, go forward 3
A tarred road: you run off, go back 2
You sink between sand grains
A leaf catches you: wait one turn
Hot sun: you evaporate, back to START
A grassy field: soak in, go forward 2
A tin roof: you run into a drain, go back 3
A johad slows you down: soak in, go forward 3
You trickle down through gravel
A borewell pumps too fast: go back 2
A thirsty root drinks you: miss a turn
You seep sideways through the rock
A tiled courtyard: run off, go back 2
A village pond: sink in slowly, go forward 1
A rooftop pipe takes you to a recharge pit: soak in, go forward 2
Someone leaves a tap running: back to START
A tanka catches you: go forward 2
You join the groundwater
You find a crack in the well wall
WELL: you made it!

story.title: The Frog Who Looked Up
text: I am a frog, and I live at the bottom of a well. You have heard what people say about frogs like me. 'A frog in a well,' they say, 'thinks the whole world is a circle of sky.' I used to think that was unkind. Now I think it was only half true.

My well is old, older than anyone in the village of Bhopalpura, at the edge of the dry hills in Rajasthan. Its walls are made of stones fitted together without mortar, and moss grows in the cracks, and the circle of sky at the top is so far away that on a clear day it looks like a blue coin. All my life I have looked up at that coin and waited. Water, I believed, came from there. When the rains came, the sky turned grey, and drops fell down the well and splashed on my back, and I was sure that was where the water came from: straight down from the sky into my well.
But that year, the water stopped.

It happened slowly. Every summer the water fell lower, and every monsoon it rose a little less. Then came a summer when the water dropped below the last stone, and then below the mud, and I was left in a small damp crack at the very bottom, with only a few beetles for company.

Every morning a girl called Kesar came with her mother to the well. I could see their two heads, small and black against the blue coin. They let down the bucket on its rope and it came back up with nothing but a little mud. Kesar dropped a pebble once, to hear the splash. There was no splash. I heard her mother say, 'Chalo. The tanker comes to the road at nine.' And their heads went away, and I knew they would walk a long way in the heat and wait in a long line, and carry the water home on their heads.

Then the monsoon came. I sat in my crack and looked up and waited for the sky to fill my well. The rain came hard. I heard it drumming on the hills. Drops fell into the well and splashed on my back, and I sang. But it was not enough. Only the drops that fell exactly into the little circle at the top reached me. I could hear something else too, a rushing, roaring sound far away. Later I understood: the rain was falling on the bare, hard hills above the village, where the goats had eaten every blade of grass and the trees had been cut for firewood. The rain could not get into that hard ground. It ran off in brown streams, down the road, past the village, past my well, and away. In two days the rushing stopped, and the sun came out, and my well was still dry.

That winter, I heard new sounds above. Thump. Thump. Scrape. Thump. Voices, many of them, women's voices mostly, and children laughing, and someone singing. Day after day the thumping went on. Kesar came to the well less often now, and when she did, her hands were red with earth, and she was smiling.
'What are they doing up there?' I asked a beetle. Beetles don't know anything.

Much later I learned what it was. An old woman in the village remembered that, long ago, there had been a johad at the foot of the hill: a long, curved bank of earth, like a smile, that caught the rain before it could run away. Over the years it had crumbled and been forgotten. Now the women of Bhopalpura were building it again, basket by basket, and Kesar carried the smallest basket of all.

The next monsoon came. I looked up at the circle of sky. The rain fell, and some drops fell into the well, and I sang, but not many. Then the rain stopped, and the sun came out. I sat in my crack, and I waited, and nothing came down.
And then, one night, the wall beside me began to feel cold.

I pressed my side against the stones. They were wet. Not wet from above. Wet from inside. A thin trickle of water was coming out of a crack between two stones, not falling, but seeping, sideways, out of the earth itself. Then another crack began to weep, and another. In the morning there was a puddle at the bottom of the well. By the next week, the water covered my back. By the end of the month it was halfway up the wall, cold and clear and tasting of stone, and it had not come from the sky at all. It had come from the side. It had come from below.

I swam up and down my well in wonder. All my life I had looked up. All my life the water had been all around me, in the dark ground on every side, moving so slowly that I never felt it, soaking down from the hills and the fields and from the new pond behind Kesar's smile of earth, and finding its way through the soil and the cracks in the rock, to me.
The next morning two heads appeared against the blue coin. The bucket came down on its rope and landed with a slap right beside me, and came up full.
'Amma!' I heard Kesar shout. 'There's a frog in it!'

She tipped me gently back into the water, and I sank down, and looked up at her face in the circle of sky. Then I looked at the walls, and the wet stones, and the dark earth beyond them. I am still a frog in a well. But I know now that my well is not a hole in the ground. It is a window.
story.epiphany: The frog believes water comes straight down from the sky into the well, so it keeps looking up. The turn comes when the well fills from the sides and below. The johad held the rain back, so it soaked into the ground and travelled through it as groundwater. The idea hidden in the story: rain that soaks in is not lost. It is stored underground and refills wells, and slowing rain down lets it soak in.
ask: Where did the frog think water came from? Where did it really come from in the end?
Why didn't the heavy rain on the bare hills fill the well?
What did the johad do to the rain?
Who built the johad? Why do you think the story mentions the smallest basket?
What does the frog mean when it says the well is a window?

ideas.idea: Rain does one of three things when it lands.
ideas.more: It soaks into the ground, it runs off to drains, rivers and the sea, or it evaporates into the air as invisible water vapour. The sun-and-shade plates, the surfaces test and the jar well each show one of these.

ideas.idea: The ground stores water in the gaps between grains of soil and rock.
ideas.more: This is groundwater. Wells and borewells are holes into it. It refills slowly from rain that soaks in, so paving over soil and cutting forests can dry up wells even when the rain is good. That is why Tamil Nadu has made every new building catch its rainwater and send it into the ground.

ideas.idea: Clear is not the same as clean.
ideas.more: Water can look clear and still carry germs or dissolved salts. That is why John Snow's map mattered. People trusted the Broad Street pump because its water tasted good.

ideas.idea: Water is shared by everything alive.
ideas.more: The same groundwater feeds neighbours' wells, tree roots, ponds and frogs. When one person pumps too much, others go dry. Ask: can one person own water?

unknowns: Where did Earth's water come from in the first place? Some scientists think icy comets or asteroids brought it, others think it was in the rocks the Earth was built from. Nobody knows for sure yet.

Nobody knows exactly how much groundwater is under India or how fast it is refilling. Scientists use satellites that feel tiny changes in the pull of gravity as underground water is pumped out, but the picture is still rough.

Forecasters still can't say for sure, months ahead, whether a monsoon will be good or poor. The monsoon depends on the oceans, the winds and the land all at once, and it is one of the hardest weather systems in the world to predict.
big: Who does the rain belong to: the person whose roof it falls on, the village, the river, or nobody?
Should water be free for everyone?
Is it fair if one family digs a very deep borewell and the neighbours' wells dry up?
If a frog and a farmer both need the last water in a pond, who should get it?
The water in your glass may once have been in a dinosaur, a cloud and the sea. Does that change how you feel about it?

challenge.q: The famous story says: 'When John Snow took the handle off the Broad Street pump, the cholera stopped.' Is that what happened?
challenge.hint: Not quite. By the time the handle was removed, deaths were already falling, partly because many people had fled the area. Snow himself said this. But the handle being off may have stopped a second wave: soon after, the sick baby's father also fell ill, and his waste could have gone into the same well. Snow's real proof was his careful map and his count of who drank which water. Ask: why do people like stories with one dramatic moment?

challenge.q: 'If water is clear and tastes good, it's safe to drink.'
challenge.hint: No. The Broad Street water was known for tasting good. Germs are too small to see, and some groundwater in India carries invisible arsenic or too much fluoride, which only a test can find. Ask: how could you find out if your home's water is safe?

challenge.q: 'A well is just a hole that catches rain.'
challenge.hint: Very little rain falls straight into a well. Almost all the water in a well seeps in from the groundwater all around it, which was rain that soaked into the land, sometimes far away and months or years before. Ask: what does that mean for wells in a village where all the land is paved?

perspectives.who: A woman in a dry village who fetches water
perspectives.view: In many parts of rural India, women and girls walk to a well, pond or handpump every day and carry water home, sometimes for hours. When a village gets taps in each home, girls often have more time for school. Ask: who in your home spends the most time on water?

perspectives.who: A family in the Thar desert with a tanka
perspectives.view: They keep the courtyard around their underground tank swept and clean, because every drop of rain that falls on it runs into the tank and will be drunk for months. Ask: what would you do differently if your roof was your drinking-water source?

perspectives.who: A crow on a city balcony in May
perspectives.view: In the hottest months, birds and squirrels in cities struggle to find water, because ponds have been filled in and drains are covered. Ask: if the crow could talk, what would it say about how we use water?

A plumber knows the hidden map of every building: where the water comes in, where it leaks, where it goes out. Ask: why is the plumber's job important, and why do we only notice it when something breaks?

books.title: Water Is Water
books.author: Miranda Paul (illustrated by Jason Chin)
books.why: A simple walk through rain, steam, fog, ice and back again. A gentle first look at the water cycle, which comes properly in Class 5.

books.title: The Water Princess
books.author: Susan Verde (illustrated by Peter H. Reynolds)
books.why: Based on the childhood of Georgie Badiel in Burkina Faso, who walked every day with her mother to fetch water. Pairs with Day 3's 'Who brings the water?'

books.title: A Drop Around the World
books.author: Barbara Shaw McKinney
books.why: Follows one drop of water through clouds, rivers, plants and animals around the world.

books.title: One Well: The Story of Water on Earth
books.author: Rochelle Strauss
books.why: Shows all the water on Earth as one shared well, with clear facts about how much we use and who has too little.

check.q: What three things can rain do when it lands?
check.a: Soak into the ground, run off over the surface, or evaporate into the air.

check.q: What is groundwater, and how does a well get water?
check.a: Water stored in the tiny gaps between soil, sand and rock underground. It seeps into the well from the sides and bottom.

check.q: Where does the water in our home come from?
check.a: Your child names your real source from the pipe trail: a river, lake or dam, a borewell, or a tanker.

check.q: Why does a clay pot keep water cool?
check.a: Water seeps through the clay and evaporates from the outside, which takes heat away.

check.q: We filtered muddy water and it came out clear. Why shouldn't we drink it?
check.a: It can still have germs too small to see. Boiling or a proper purifier makes it safe.

check.q: Name two ways to reuse or save water at home.
check.a: For example: rice water for plants, last rinse water for mopping, closing the tap while brushing, fixing drips.

check.q: Why did the frog's well fill up again?
check.a: The johad held the rain back so it soaked into the ground and refilled the groundwater, which seeped into the well.
